content.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

blocks.text: Problem Summary: An array of distinct values, originally sorted in ascending order, has been rotated at some unknown pivot. Given this rotated array nums, find its minimum value in O(log n) time.

blocks.text: An array of distinct values, originally sorted in ascending order, has been rotated at some unknown pivot. Given this rotated array nums, find its minimum value in O(log n) time.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Clock Face Cut and Reattached
blocks.text: Picture a sorted number line bent into a circle and then cut open at a random point to be laid flat again. The smallest value sits exactly at the point where the circle was cut, right where a larger value suddenly drops to a smaller one.

blocks.caption: The array is sorted but rotated, the minimum sits right at the rotation point

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The drop from 5 down to 1 marks the rotation point","the minimum sits right after the drop","a rotation always creates exactly one place where a larger value is immediately followed by a smaller one"],["Answer","1","the value right after the drop is the smallest in the array"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The drop from 7 down to 0 marks the rotation point","the minimum sits right after the drop","a rotation always creates exactly one place where a larger value is immediately followed by a smaller one"],["Answer","0","the value right after the drop is the smallest in the array"]]}

blocks.text: If the array happens to have zero effective rotation, it is already fully sorted, so the minimum is simply its first element, 11.
It helps to ask what "sorted, then rotated" actually preserves, since that structure is exactly what a faster search should exploit.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A plain linear scan finds the minimum correctly but completely ignores that the array is sorted apart from a single rotation point, information the problem specifically hands over.

Observation 2: Sqrt(x) already showed that binary search does not require comparing the middle to an exact target value; it can instead ask a yes or no question and discard half the search space based on the answer.

Observation 3: Here that question becomes "does the rotation point lie in the left half or the right half of the current range", answered by comparing the middle element to the rightmost element: if the middle is greater than the rightmost, a wraparound drop must exist somewhere in the right half.

Observation 4: Tracing nums equal to [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] confirms it, each comparison of mid against the rightmost value correctly halves the range and converges on index 4, holding the true minimum, 0.
Treating "sorted but rotated" as a structural clue, rather than noise that breaks binary search, is what turns an O(n) scan into an O(log n) search.
Scan the entire array once, keeping track of the smallest value seen.

items: Walk through every element of the array.
Keep track of the smallest value seen so far.
Return that value once the scan finishes.

codes.python:
def find_min(nums):
    smallest = nums[0]
    for num in nums:                                        # check every value directly
        smallest = min(smallest, num)
    return smallest


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]
    print(find_min(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The running minimum starts at the first element, so a single element array is already handled correctly with no special case.
Every element is compared against the running minimum in one linear pass, regardless of where the rotation point happens to be.
This approach never looks at the sorted structure of the array at all, treating it as if it were in arbitrary order.

blocks.text: Checking every value directly is guaranteed to find the true minimum.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a full linear scan.
Space: O(1), only the running minimum is kept.

Limitation: this completely ignores the fact that the array is sorted apart from a single rotation point, information that should make it possible to locate the minimum in logarithmic time instead of linear.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the linear scan works but is wasteful: it treats a mostly sorted array exactly like a completely unsorted one, throwing away the one piece of structure the problem guarantees.

What binary search on a boundary comparison fixes directly: comparing the middle element to the rightmost element tells us, in one comparison, which half of the current range still contains the rotation point.

Why the rightmost element specifically: if nums[mid] is greater than nums[right], every value from mid to right must have wrapped around at least once, so the drop, and the minimum, must be strictly after mid.

The core idea: repeatedly halve the search range using that single comparison, always keeping the half that must still contain the rotation point, until left and right converge on the minimum itself.

Use binary search, guided by comparing the middle element to the rightmost element rather than the usual comparison to a target value. If the middle element is greater than the rightmost element, the rotation point (and therefore the minimum) must be somewhere in the right half, so search there. Otherwise, the right half is already fully sorted and the minimum is at or before the middle, so search the left half including the middle itself.
Binary search comparing the middle element against the rightmost element to decide which half contains the rotation point.

blocks.caption: Optimized: binary search comparing the middle value to the rightmost value

blocks.text: This works because in any sorted-then-rotated array, comparing the middle element to the rightmost element always correctly identifies which half still contains the rotation point: a middle greater than the rightmost means the right half wraps around, while a middle less than or equal to the rightmost means the right half is already fully sorted and the rotation point is at or before the middle.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["nums[mid] is greater than nums[right]","The right half must contain the wraparound drop","left moves to mid plus 1, discarding the left half"],["nums[mid] is less than or equal to nums[right]","The right half is already fully sorted, so the minimum is at or before mid","right moves to mid, keeping mid itself as a candidate"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), the search space is halved on every step.
Space: O(1), only a couple of index variables are kept.

blocks.text: This is the standard "modified binary search on a rotated sorted array" pattern: instead of comparing the middle to a search target, compare it to one of the boundaries to decide which half is guaranteed to still be properly sorted, then recurse into whichever half must contain the answer.

items: Comparing the middle element to the leftmost element instead of the rightmost, which does not reliably distinguish which half contains the rotation point.
Setting right equal to mid minus 1 instead of mid, which can accidentally skip over the minimum itself when it happens to sit at the middle position.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "the array is sorted but rotated", think: modified binary search, compare the middle to a boundary instead of a target.
If the interviewer says "what if there could be duplicate values", think: the comparison can become ambiguous when nums[mid] equals nums[right], requiring a linear step to break the tie in the worst case.
If the interviewer says "can you find a target value in this rotated array", think: this same rotation point detection extends into full rotated array search.

What would break if right were set to mid minus 1 instead of mid?
How would you find the number of times the array has been rotated, given only the array itself?
Sqrt(x), whose binary search eliminates half the range based on a yes or no comparison rather than an exact match, the same instinct applied here to a boundary instead of a target.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array, which extends this exact rotation point detection to locate an arbitrary target value, not just the minimum.

Any problem describing data as "sorted, then something applied to it" (rotated, shifted, or otherwise transformed), where a modified binary search comparison against a boundary is usually the fastest approach.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: modified binary search, comparing the middle element to a boundary element instead of to a search target.

Core Idea: comparing nums[mid] to nums[right] reveals which half of the range still contains the rotation point, letting binary search eliminate half the array on every step even without a target value to search for.
Time: O(n) for the brute force, O(log n) for the optimized binary search.
Space: O(1) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: binary search only needs a comparison that reliably eliminates half the search space, it does not require searching for an exact target value.
Interview Difficulty: the overall structure is standard; correctly choosing the right boundary to compare against, and using right equals mid rather than mid minus 1, is where most mistakes happen.
One line memory trick: compare the middle to the rightmost value, the greater one points toward the rotation point.
